title: EZEKIEL 23 MAY BE THE MOST SEXUALLY GRAPHIC CHAPTER MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER READ
paragraphs: EZEKIEL 23 MAY BE THE MOST SEXUALLY GRAPHIC CHAPTER MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER READ
The chapter is shocking. The Hebrew is uncomfortable. But if you stop at the sexual imagery, you may completely miss the terrifying—and ultimately Gospel-shaped—truth Ezekiel was trying to expose.
There are chapters of the Bible we frame on walls.
There are verses we put on coffee mugs.
There are passages we underline in beautiful colors and send to friends when they are hurting.
A chapter so sexually explicit, so violent, so uncomfortable, that many Christians can spend years in church without ever hearing a sermon devoted to it.
Read it carefully and you may understand why.
It is the kind of chapter that can make a sincere Christian wonder:
Why is this in the Bible?
And perhaps an even more unsettling question:
Why did God allow His prophet to speak this graphically?
Before going any further, something must be said clearly.
Ezekiel 23 must never be twisted into permission to degrade women, shame survivors of sexual violence, excuse abuse, or suggest that victims are responsible for what perpetrators have done to them.
The women in this prophetic allegory are not two ordinary women whose private sexual lives God decided to publicly humiliate.
God tells us exactly whom they represent.
Their names are Oholah and Oholibah.
Oholah represents Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
Oholibah represents Jerusalem, capital of Judah.
They are cities portrayed as sisters.
Political and spiritual betrayal portrayed through adultery.
This is prophetic metaphor—and it is deliberately disturbing.
The Hebrew does not soften it.
The verb comes from the Hebrew root זנה — zanah, a word associated with prostitution or sexual unfaithfulness and frequently employed by the prophets as imagery for covenant infidelity.
The remainder of the verse describes their breasts being handled in their youth.
Later the imagery becomes even more graphic.
Because Ezekiel is not writing pornography.
And God wants His people to feel something they had apparently stopped feeling:
Because beneath all the sexual language is the story of a broken covenant.
Yet repeatedly they chased the gods of surrounding nations and placed their confidence in foreign powers rather than the Lord.
The language of adultery therefore makes sense within the Bible's covenant world.
This wasn't merely someone breaking an arbitrary religious regulation.
Perhaps that is why sanitized language would not have carried the same weight.
“My wife violated clause seven of our marital agreement.”
And Ezekiel wants Israel to understand that idolatry is not spiritually harmless.
It is not simply “exploring another path.”
It is giving to something created what belongs to the Creator.
The tragedy becomes even clearer in the names themselves.
אָהֳלָה — Oholah is commonly understood in connection with “her tent.”
אָהֳלִיבָה — Oholibah carries the sense of “My tent is in her.”
His “tent,” so to speak, was among His people.
Yet having the temple nearby did not mean their hearts were near God.
Because you can be surrounded by sacred things and still give your heart to idols.
You can own five Bibles and ignore the voice of God.
You can sing worship songs while secretly worshiping approval.
You can raise your hands on Sunday and spend Monday bowing before money.
You can post Scripture publicly while feeding lust privately.
You can defend Christian morality online while refusing to forgive someone in your own home.
You can know the language of grace without surrendering the hidden room.
And suddenly Ezekiel 23 stops being about “those disgusting people thousands of years ago.”
That is when the chapter becomes uncomfortable in an entirely different way.
We may not kneel before carved statues.
Some before the desperate need to be admired.
Some before an image of themselves carefully constructed for strangers on a screen.
Anything can become an idol when it receives the trust, obedience, identity, or devotion that belongs ultimately to God.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that idolatry rarely introduces itself by saying:
Hello. I am here to replace God.
And bondage eventually starts feeling normal.
That is the nightmare Ezekiel exposes.
The chapter's sexual imagery becomes progressively degrading because sin itself is degrading.
What promises freedom eventually demands payment.
What promises intimacy eventually leaves emptiness.
What promises control eventually becomes a master.
The “lovers” Israel chased would eventually become instruments of her destruction.
That is one of the darkest ironies in the chapter.
She ran toward the very powers that would consume her.
And haven't we done something painfully similar?
We run to something because we believe it will heal us.
Then one day we discover we need healing from the thing we ran to.
Then the door closed behind us.
This is why biblical warnings about sin are not evidence that God hates pleasure.
They are evidence that God sees where counterfeit pleasure eventually leads.
Near the end of the chapter, God identifies sins underneath the metaphor that cannot be dismissed as merely sexual imagery.
There is blood on their hands.
There is the sacrifice of children.
There is desecration of God's sanctuary.
There is profanation of His Sabbaths.
They could slaughter their children before idols and then enter God's sanctuary.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that more than another inspirational quote.
Jesus did not die so we could become better actors.
He died to make sinners new.
Christianity is not learning how to look clean while protecting whatever is killing you in secret.
The Gospel invites you into the light.
But light also shows you the door.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch when you're alone.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages.
Maybe nobody knows how much you drink.
Maybe nobody knows what you fantasize about.
Maybe nobody knows how bitter you have become.
Maybe everyone thinks your marriage is fine.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is strong.
Maybe you have become frighteningly good at saying,
Ezekiel 23 is not permission for Christians to stand above broken people and shout,
If that is what we take from this chapter, we have missed the mirror.
Scripture exposes sin so that sinners will stop hiding from the God who alone can save them.
And this is where we must read Ezekiel from this side of the cross.
Jesus reveals how far God will go to redeem covenant breakers.
The Bible does not end in Ezekiel 23.
Eventually another scandal unfolds outside Jerusalem.
But this time the shame does not belong to Him.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, carries what sinners could never cleanse themselves from.
As the apostle Peter would later write:
The betrayed God comes for the betrayer.
The Holy One comes for the unclean.
The faithful Bridegroom comes for an unfaithful people.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin was so serious that redemption required blood.
Yet grace was so astonishing that Christ willingly shed His own.
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
“Repent. Come to Christ. Stop hiding. Mercy has a name.”
This does not turn grace into permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Jesus told the woman caught in adultery that He did not condemn her—and then called her away from her life of sin.
Maybe pornography has owned years of your life.
Maybe you are carrying secret shame from something you did years ago.
Maybe something was done to you, and religious people made you believe that another person's evil somehow made you dirty before God.
Your abuse was not your sin.
Your wounds are not evidence that God despises you.
Maybe your idol isn't sexual at all.
Because the message underneath Ezekiel's shocking imagery is not merely:
Look how desperately we need a Savior.
He doesn't need the edited version of your testimony.
He already knows the unedited one.
Every room you hope nobody enters.
Not because your sin doesn't matter.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
One drives you deeper into darkness.
The other leads you toward repentance.
And perhaps that is why Ezekiel 23 remains in our Bible.
God loves us too much to sanitize the ugliness of rebellion.
He tells the truth about sin.
Then the larger biblical story tells us the astonishing truth about grace.
Maybe you started reading because somebody told you Ezekiel 23 was one of the Bible's most sexually graphic chapters.
But perhaps conviction kept you here.
Bring trusted, mature believers into the struggle where appropriate.
Stop feeding whatever keeps starving your soul.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't have to describe your private sin publicly.
As a small declaration that darkness will not have the final word.

And invite your family, your Christian friends, the believer who has grown cold, the person struggling secretly, the seeker asking difficult questions—even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about human brokenness—to come with you.

Supporting Gospel ministry is not a way to purchase God's favor, prove that you glorify God, or earn spiritual blessing. Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased. Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Not because clicking “share” makes somebody righteous.
Someone may be trapped in pornography.
Someone may be hiding an affair.
Someone may believe they have gone too far for God to want them.
And your share could put one sentence in front of them at exactly the moment they need it:
Jesus still receives sinners who come home.
Ezekiel 23 is disturbing because sin is disturbing.
The cross is scandalous because grace is scandalous.
And the empty tomb announces that neither your darkest chapter nor your deepest shame has authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Receive the mercy you cannot earn.
And follow the Savior who does more than cover scandals.
The chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read may become the very page where Jesus begins rewriting your story.
